q1.prompt: When you ask CoCo a business question, what does it actually give you back?

a.text: SQL you read, run, and verify yourself
a.feedback: Correct! CoCo writes the SQL — you stay accountable for reading, running, and checking it.

b.text: A final answer you can trust without checking
b.feedback: Not quite — CoCo is fast, but you verify the result. The lab's whole 'trust but verify' step exists for this reason.

c.text: A chart only, with no underlying query
c.feedback: CoCo writes the SQL behind the answer — you can read and modify it.

d.text: A change to the underlying data
d.feedback: Asking a question runs a read query; it doesn't change the data.

q2.prompt: Most of the questions in this lab were answered by the same SQL shape. What is it?

a.text: SELECT ... FROM ... JOIN ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ... ORDER BY
a.feedback: Correct! Change the grouping column or the table and the same pattern answers a new question.

b.feedback: That builds a new table — these were read-only questions using SELECT/JOIN/GROUP BY.

c.feedback: That writes rows — the lab only queried existing data.

d.feedback: That's access control (Lab 3). Here you were querying data.

q3.prompt: You asked CoCo to show only stores with an average score below 4. Which clause does that filtering, and why?

a.text: HAVING — it filters groups after GROUP BY
a.feedback: Correct! AVG(score) is computed per group, so the threshold has to be applied with HAVING, after grouping.

b.text: WHERE — it filters the grouped averages
b.feedback: WHERE runs before grouping, so it can't see AVG(score). The group-level filter is HAVING.

c.text: ORDER BY — it drops the rows you don't want
c.feedback: ORDER BY only sorts; it doesn't remove rows.

d.text: LIMIT — it keeps only the low scorers
d.feedback: LIMIT caps the row count regardless of value; it can't filter by a computed average.

q5.prompt: You type '@PLATPLUS_DB.ROASTERY_SALES' before your question in CoCo. What does this do?

a.text: Grants CoCo permission to query that database
a.feedback: The @ reference is about context, not permissions — your role already determines what you can query.

b.text: Gives CoCo the actual table names and column names so it writes accurate SQL instead of guessing
b.feedback: Correct! The @ picker grounds CoCo in your real schema — it can see the tables and columns and write SQL that actually runs.

c.text: Switches your session to that database automatically
c.feedback: USE DATABASE changes your session context; @ in CoCo is about giving the AI schema context, not switching your session.

d.text: Searches the Marketplace for matching datasets
d.feedback: That's the Marketplace tab. @ in the CoCo prompt is the schema/object picker for grounding your question.

q6.prompt: You load the roastery-analyst skill before asking CoCo a question. What changes?

a.text: CoCo runs faster because it skips schema discovery
a.feedback: Speed isn't the main benefit. The skill changes what CoCo *knows*, not how fast it runs.

b.text: CoCo has pre-loaded schema context and business knowledge, so it can answer domain-specific questions accurately without needing @ references
b.feedback: Correct! A skill packages reusable context — schema, business definitions, common patterns — so the whole team benefits from it, not just the person who built it.

c.text: CoCo switches to a more powerful AI model
c.feedback: Skills don't change the underlying model — they add structured context that makes the model more useful for your specific domain.

d.text: CoCo gains write access to your database
d.feedback: Skills add knowledge context; database permissions are still controlled by your Snowflake role, not by CoCo.

q7.prompt: In the Data Engineer section, you created a dynamic table instead of running a query. What is the key difference?

a.text: A dynamic table stores a fixed snapshot that you have to refresh manually
a.feedback: That's a static table. A dynamic table refreshes automatically based on TARGET_LAG — no manual refresh needed.

b.text: A dynamic table is a persisted, auto-refreshing result set — the query runs on a schedule so the data stays current without manual reruns
b.feedback: Correct! TARGET_LAG tells Snowflake how fresh the result needs to be. The DE doesn't run the query again — it just queries the dynamic table and gets current results.

c.text: A dynamic table is faster than a regular query because it caches the warehouse
c.feedback: Performance isn't the main point. The value is automation — results stay fresh without someone running the query manually every day.

d.text: A dynamic table can only be queried by the role that created it
d.feedback: Dynamic tables follow normal Snowflake RBAC — you can GRANT SELECT on them to other roles, just like any table.
